title: THE BIBLE LEFT IT UNSAID. WHY ARE WE PUTTING WORDS IN GOD’S MOUTH?
paragraphs: THE BIBLE LEFT IT UNSAID. WHY ARE WE PUTTING WORDS IN GOD’S MOUTH?
The dangerous moment when imagination becomes revelation, assumptions become doctrine, and a story God never told begins to sound more convincing than the truth He actually gave us.
There is something deeply unsettling about realizing that you may have believed a Bible story your entire life… only to discover that part of the story was never actually in the Bible.
Not because someone deliberately lied to you.
Not because you stopped loving Jesus.
But because somewhere along the way, a preacher's illustration became a remembered detail. A movie scene became a biblical memory. A familiar tradition became something you were certain God had said.
And nobody thought to ask the most important question.
Where does Scripture actually say that?
That question can make people uncomfortable.
Especially when the story is beautiful.
Especially when it makes us cry.
Especially when we've heard it preached since childhood.
But what happens when a story moves our hearts while quietly teaching us to believe something God never revealed?
What happens when our desire to make Scripture more dramatic begins to compete with our responsibility to keep Scripture true?
And here is the question that should stop every Christian writer, preacher, content creator, Bible teacher, and believer in their tracks:
If God deliberately chose not to tell us something, what gives us the authority to speak as though He did?
Stay with me, because this is not merely about correcting a few Bible stories.
This is about whether we love the voice of God enough to stop speaking when He has stopped speaking.
And it is about a Savior whose true story is already so extraordinary that we do not need to invent a single detail to make Him glorious.
Think about Mary Magdalene.
How many times have you heard someone confidently describe her as a prostitute before Jesus rescued her?
How many sermons have painted a detailed picture of her former lifestyle, her supposed customers, her shameful encounters, and the moment she allegedly abandoned prostitution to follow Christ?
It makes a dramatic testimony.
The problem?
The Bible never identifies Mary Magdalene as a prostitute.
Luke 8:2 tells us that Mary, called Magdalene, was a woman from whom seven demons had gone out.
The Greek text says:
Μαρία ἡ καλουμένη Μαγδαληνή, ἀφ’ ἧς δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ ἐξεληλύθει.
A faithful translation is:
"Mary, who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out."
That is what Luke tells us.
Seven demons.
Deliverance.
A woman whose life had been touched by the liberating power of Jesus Christ.
But Luke does not tell us she was a prostitute.
He does not identify her as the unnamed sinful woman in Luke 7.
He does not provide a detailed account of her life before her deliverance.
Yet over centuries, those separate accounts became intertwined in popular Christian imagination.
And eventually, many people stopped distinguishing between what the Bible revealed and what tradition supplied.
Now consider the terrible irony.
In trying to magnify the grace of Jesus, we may have attached an unverified sexual history to a real woman whom Scripture honors as a devoted follower of Christ and a witness to His resurrection.
Mary Magdalene does not need an invented scandal to make her redemption remarkable.
Being delivered by Jesus was remarkable enough.
Following Him was remarkable enough.
Standing near the cross when others had fled was remarkable enough.
Hearing the risen Christ call her by name in John 20 was remarkable enough.
Her true story is already overflowing with grace.
Why would we need to give her another one?
And perhaps this is where the issue becomes personal.
Because many of us have done something similar without realizing it.
We have told people that the forbidden fruit in Eden was an apple.
But Genesis never identifies the fruit as an apple.
We have described three wise men visiting baby Jesus in the manger.
But Matthew 2 does not give the number of the Magi, and it describes their visit to a house. Three gifts are named, but three visitors are not.

We have imagined Jonah sitting comfortably inside a whale, even though the Hebrew of Jonah 1:17 identifies the creature as a דָּג גָּדוֹל (dag gadol)—a great fish. The account does not provide the creature's biological species or a detailed description of Jonah's surroundings.

We have heard people confidently describe the physical appearance of Jesus, the exact tone of His voice, the expression on His face during particular conversations, and even His private thoughts at moments when the Gospels give us no such information.
Some of these details are harmless when clearly presented as artistic imagination.
Others can seriously distort our understanding of Scripture.
The danger begins when we stop saying, "Perhaps it happened this way," and start declaring, "This is what happened."
Because there is an enormous difference between imagining a scene to help someone understand a biblical event and claiming that God has revealed details He never gave us.
One is an illustration.
The other can become a false assertion about divine revelation.
And Scripture does not treat that distinction lightly.
Deuteronomy 4:2 warns Israel not to add to or take away from God's commandments.
The Hebrew begins:
לֹא תֹסִפוּ עַל־הַדָּבָר
Lo tosifu al-hadavar.
"You shall not add to the word."
In context, Moses is warning Israel against altering the commandments God has given them.
This verse is not a prohibition against every form of creative storytelling or historical investigation.
But its underlying concern is unmistakable: God's people must not presume authority to modify what God has commanded.
Proverbs 30:5–6 carries a closely related warning.
"Every word of God is pure."
And then:
"Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar."
That is the King James rendering.
Notice the seriousness.
Not merely that someone might be mistaken.
Not merely that an illustration might become exaggerated.
But that adding words to God's revelation can turn a person who intends to communicate truth into someone who misrepresents it.
And if we claim to love the Lord, that should matter to us.
Deeply.
Because the goal of Christian storytelling is not to make people believe we have an extraordinary imagination.
The goal is to help people encounter the extraordinary truth of Jesus Christ.
And the truth does not become more powerful when we decorate it with certainty we do not possess.
Now think about the woman caught in adultery in John 7:53–8:11.
It is one of the most emotionally gripping accounts traditionally included in the Gospel of John.
A woman stands accused.
Religious leaders surround her.
The threat of judgment hangs over the scene.
And Jesus bends down and writes on the ground.
What did He write?
For generations, people have offered dramatic answers.
Some say He wrote the secret sins of the accusers.
Others say He wrote their names.
Still others suggest He wrote specific commandments or accusations.
But the passage does not tell us what He wrote.
The Greek of John 8:6 says:
κατέγραφεν εἰς τὴν γῆν.
"He was writing on the ground."
That is the information the text provides.

And there is another important matter that responsible Bible teaching must acknowledge: this entire passage has a complex manuscript history. It is absent from many of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John, and modern Bible editions commonly mark it with a textual note.
Christians have discussed its historical authenticity and canonical status for centuries.
We should not conceal that complexity from readers.
Yet even when discussing the account as traditionally received, one fact remains:
The passage never reveals what Jesus wrote.
We may explore possibilities.
We may discuss interpretations.
We may even portray a possible scene in a clearly identified work of historical fiction.
But we cannot honestly tell people that Jesus wrote the accusers' hidden sins as though the biblical author had disclosed it.
Imagine standing before Christ one day and discovering that the detail you preached with absolute confidence was never part of His revealed Word.
Wouldn't you wish you had simply said, "The Bible doesn't tell us"?
Those six words are not evidence of weak faith.
Sometimes they are evidence of reverence.
Sometimes the most faithful sentence a Bible teacher can speak is:
"I don't know, because Scripture doesn't say."
And that is not a failure of biblical understanding.
That is biblical understanding recognizing its own limits.
But there is something even more important here.
Something that reaches beyond storytelling into the deepest parts of our spiritual lives.
We often struggle with what God has not told us because we struggle with what God has not explained to us.
We want to know why a prayer remains unanswered.
Why a loved one died.
Why a faithful Christian suffered.
Why a marriage collapsed.
Why a child wandered away from the faith.
Why God permitted something that left us on the floor, exhausted, trembling, and unable to understand what came next.
We want details.
We want explanations.
We want a complete picture.
And when heaven seems silent, we sometimes become desperate to fill the silence ourselves.
We tell ourselves that every painful event must have one specific hidden reason we can identify.
We assign motives to God that He has not disclosed.
We promise people outcomes He has not promised.
We confidently declare that a particular tragedy happened because God was teaching someone a specific lesson.
But how do we know?
Sometimes we don't.
And we should be careful.
The friends of Job made this mistake.
They looked at a suffering man and constructed explanations for his suffering.
Their arguments sounded religious.
Their speeches were full of moral certainty.
They believed they understood the connection between Job's circumstances and God's justice.
But they did not possess the heavenly perspective revealed to the reader in Job 1–2.
And in Job 42:7, the Lord rebuked them for failing to speak rightly about Him.
Let that sink in.
It is possible to say many religious things about God and still speak wrongly about God.
It is possible to sound spiritually confident while being biblically careless.
It is possible to speak with tears in your eyes and sincerity in your heart and still attribute something to God that He never said.
Sincerity matters.
But sincerity does not turn an assumption into revelation.
This is why Deuteronomy 29:29 is so profoundly important.
The Hebrew says:
הַנִּסְתָּרֹת לַיהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ וְהַנִּגְלֹת לָנוּ וּלְבָנֵינוּ
Hanistarot la-YHWH Eloheinu, vehaniglot lanu ulevaneinu.
"The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children..."
The verse continues by connecting what has been revealed with obedience to God's law.
Do you see the distinction?
There are things God has revealed.
And there are things He has not.
The revealed things are given to us so that we may know, believe, and obey.
The hidden things belong to Him.
Not to our imagination.
Not to our speculative certainty.
Not to the preacher with the most dramatic voice.
Not to the Christian content creator who knows which emotional details will make a story go viral.
To Him.
And perhaps one of the most beautiful expressions of spiritual maturity is learning to trust God without demanding possession of everything He has chosen not to reveal.
But please understand something.
This does not mean Christian writers must abandon creativity.
The Bible itself contains poetry, parables, metaphor, vivid imagery, dramatic dialogue, and extraordinary literary artistry.
Jesus used stories to communicate truth.
He spoke of a father welcoming a lost son.
A shepherd searching for a lost sheep.
A Samaritan stopping beside a wounded stranger.
These were not boring, emotionally empty presentations.
They were unforgettable.
They pierced the conscience.
They exposed hypocrisy.
They revealed mercy.
They invited repentance.
And they still move hearts thousands of years later.
The issue is not whether storytelling should be powerful.
The issue is whether we are honest about the difference between God's story and our storytelling.
A writer may say, "Imagine how Peter might have felt when the rooster crowed."
That is a clearly signaled invitation to reflect.
But the writer should not manufacture an elaborate private conversation between Peter and Jesus and present it as an event recorded in the Gospels.
A preacher may explore the emotional significance of the prodigal son's return.
But he should not invent the son's exact words, additional sins, or the father's private history and teach them as though Luke recorded those details.
A Christian filmmaker may dramatize the atmosphere of a biblical scene.
But the audience should be able to distinguish artistic additions from the biblical account.
Creativity can serve the truth.
But it must never quietly replace the truth.
And this matters especially in a world where dramatic religious content can spread across millions of screens before anyone checks whether the claims are biblical.
A sentence can be shared ten thousand times.
A moving story can bring people to tears.
A beautifully edited video can make an invented scene feel more real than the written Gospel.
And before long, people begin defending the invention as though questioning it were questioning God.
That is how tradition can become confused with revelation.
That is how speculation can become confused with doctrine.
That is how a sincere attempt to glorify Jesus can unintentionally obscure what Jesus actually taught.
And we should never be satisfied with that.
Because Jesus did not call His disciples to manufacture spiritual impressions.
He called them to bear witness to the truth.
In John 17:17, Jesus prayed:
"Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth."
The Greek declaration is wonderfully direct:
ὁ λόγος ὁ σὸς ἀλήθειά ἐστιν.
Ho logos ho sos alētheia estin.
"Your word is truth."
Not our embellishments.
Not our assumptions.
Not the details we wish the biblical writers had included.
His Word.
And if His Word is truth, then faithfulness to His Word must matter more than applause for our presentation.
Even when accuracy makes the story less sensational.
Even when acknowledging uncertainty makes our message sound less dramatic.
Even when a biblical correction forces us to abandon an illustration we have loved for years.
Truth is not the enemy of spiritual passion.
Truth is what gives spiritual passion its rightful foundation.
And nowhere is this more important than when we speak about the cross.
Think about what Scripture actually tells us.
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, entered our world in real human flesh.
He lived without sin.
He loved those whom others rejected.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He called sinners to repentance.
He healed the afflicted.
He welcomed the weary.
He was betrayed.
He was denied.
He was falsely accused.
He suffered under Pontius Pilate.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again according to the Scriptures.
That is not an invented drama.
That is the apostolic proclamation.
Paul summarizes the heart of this message in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
"Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures."
The Greek phrase in verse 3 is:
Χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν.
Christos apethanen hyper tōn hamartiōn hēmōn.
"Christ died for our sins."
Read that again.
For our sins.
Not merely as a tragic victim of political injustice.
Not merely as an inspirational teacher whose life ended violently.
Not merely as an example of extraordinary courage.
Christ died for our sins.
And He rose again.
Here is the scandal at the center of the Gospel.
The sinless One bore the judgment deserved by sinners.
The righteous One suffered for the unrighteous to bring us to God, as 1 Peter 3:18 declares.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and reconciliation are proclaimed to those who repent and believe.
That is grace.
Not grace manufactured by adding fictional horrors to the crucifixion.
Not grace amplified by inventing conversations between Jesus and the soldiers.
Not grace strengthened by confidently describing unrecorded details of His suffering.
Grace revealed in what God has actually made known.
And it is enough.
More than enough.
Perhaps you are reading this and realizing that you have repeated things about Scripture without checking them.
Perhaps you have shared a moving Christian story because it made you cry, never asking whether the Bible supported its details.
Perhaps you have taught a tradition as though it were a verse.
Or perhaps you are a preacher, teacher, writer, or content creator who has felt the pressure to make every message more dramatic than the last.
You want people to listen.
You want them to care.
You want them to encounter Christ.
Those desires can be good.
But there is a temptation hiding beneath them.
The temptation to believe that God's Word needs our inventions to become effective.
It does not.
The Holy Spirit does not require fabricated details to convict a sinner.
Jesus does not need a fictional past assigned to Mary Magdalene to demonstrate His power to redeem.
The resurrection does not need invented witnesses to become glorious.
The cross does not need exaggerated claims to become worthy of our worship.
And your testimony does not need embellishment to prove that God's grace is real.
If Christ rescued you from sin, tell the truth.
If He restored your life, tell the truth.
If you are still struggling, tell the truth.
If your prayers have not yet been answered, tell the truth.
If you do not understand everything God is doing, tell the truth.
A truthful testimony may sound less spectacular than a polished performance.
But it honors the God who is truth.
And for someone reading your words while quietly fighting to believe, that honesty may be exactly what they need.
Because there are people who have walked away from Christian communities after discovering that something they were confidently taught was not actually in Scripture.
There are people who feel betrayed when cherished stories turn out to contain invented details.
There are young believers trying to discern the difference between biblical teaching and religious entertainment.
And there are seekers who genuinely want to know whether Christianity can withstand careful questions.
We should not be afraid of those questions.
We should welcome them.
Christian faith is not strengthened by protecting inaccurate claims from examination.
It is strengthened when believers learn to distinguish the authority of Scripture from the fallibility of human interpretation.
And when we discover we have been wrong, repentance is not humiliation.
It is a gift.
We can correct ourselves.
We can apologize.
We can return to the text.
We can say, "I taught that as a fact, but Scripture does not actually say it. I should have been more careful."
There is no disgrace in that kind of honesty.
There is spiritual integrity.
The apostle Paul reminded Timothy in 2 Timothy 2:15 to handle the word of truth rightly.
The Greek expression includes:
ὀρθοτομοῦντα τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας.
Orthotomounta ton logon tēs alētheias.
Commonly translated as "rightly handling the word of truth."
The verb orthotomeō carries the sense of cutting straight or handling correctly.
The point is not that every teacher must know every detail of ancient languages.
The point is that God's Word deserves careful, faithful treatment.
Its context matters.
Its literary genre matters.
Its original audience matters.
Its historical setting matters.
Its actual words matter.
And the distinction between what a passage says, what it implies, what might be possible, and what remains unknown matters.
Especially when we claim to speak in God's name.
There is another danger we must resist, however.
In correcting invented details, we must not become arrogant.
Biblical accuracy is not permission to mock believers who have inherited mistaken traditions.
Knowledge without love can become another form of spiritual pride.
Some people have never been taught how to examine a passage in context.
Some grew up hearing particular stories repeated so often that they never thought to question them.
Some are simply beginning to study Scripture seriously.
They need patient correction, not humiliation.
They need truth spoken in love.
And if we are truly defending the authority of God's Word, our manner of correction should reflect the character of the Savior revealed in that Word.
Jesus was full of grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Grace and truth.
Together.
That is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not the pursuit of viral religious entertainment at the expense of biblical faithfulness.
Not emotional manipulation disguised as spiritual conviction.
Not making the Gospel more scandalous by inventing sins, scenes, and secrets.
But proclaiming the real scandal of human rebellion and the astonishing grace of Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And notice what that means.
Jesus does not rewrite history by making falsehood true.
He rewrites the future of sinners through redemption.
He brings forgiveness where there was guilt.
He brings reconciliation where there was separation.
He brings hope where there was condemnation.
He transforms people who could never save themselves.
He takes what sin has broken and begins the work of making us new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation.
That is not a literary invention.
That is a promise rooted in the saving work of Christ.
And it is more beautiful than anything we could fabricate.
So before you share your next Bible story, pause long enough to ask whether its details come from Scripture or imagination.
Before you preach a moving illustration, make sure your audience knows what is biblical and what is illustrative.
Before you repeat an unforgettable quotation attributed to Jesus, verify that He actually said it.
Before you claim to know why God allowed someone to suffer, remember Job.
Before you turn a possible interpretation into an unquestionable doctrine, remember the secret things belong to the Lord.
And before you assume that the Gospel needs another dramatic twist, return to Calvary.
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at the risen Savior.
Then ask yourself whether the truth God has revealed is really insufficient.
Because it isn't.
It never was.
And it never will be.
There is something I want to ask you personally.
Have you ever discovered that a Bible story you believed for years contained details Scripture never actually mentioned?
Or have you ever been afraid to admit, "I don't know what this passage means yet"?
You do not need to pretend you have every answer.
You do not need to defend every tradition you inherited.
You do not need to hide the fact that you are still learning.
And if this exposed something you have repeated without checking, you can simply say, "I'm learning to handle God's Word more faithfully."
That kind of honesty may encourage another believer to do the same.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to start arguments.
But to encourage a generation of Christians who love the Bible enough to let it speak for itself.
There is also a meaningful way to help this ministry continue.
Every article, every biblical reflection, every resource, and every opportunity to reach another soul requires time, work, and ongoing support.
It is not a requirement for glorifying God.
It is not a replacement for supporting your local church or fulfilling your responsibilities to your family.
And it is not a guarantee of blessing or spiritual reward.
It is a voluntary act of generosity that can help sustain and expand this particular ministry.

Scripture teaches that believers may generously support those who faithfully labor in communicating God's Word. Philippians 4:15–18 describes the Philippian believers' financial partnership with Paul's ministry, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should never be compelled.
God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you to participate.
What matters is not pressure.
What matters is faithful stewardship, a willing heart, and a shared desire to see the truth of Jesus Christ proclaimed.
The resources are there to help you read, study, reflect, pray, and become more deeply rooted in the truth of God's Word.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Open your Bible with someone who has questions.
Speak the truth about Jesus with humility and love.
Those acts matter too.
Because this mission is not ultimately about building an audience.
It is about pointing people to Christ.
One day, the applause of the world will fade.
The algorithms will change.
The stories people once shared will be forgotten.
The platforms we depend on may disappear.
But the Word of our God will stand forever.
So let us be Christians who refuse to trade truth for attention.
Writers who refuse to confuse imagination with revelation.
Teachers who are willing to say, "Scripture does not tell us."
Believers who are humble enough to be corrected.
Disciples who would rather have a faithful understanding of God's Word than a spectacular story built on details God never gave.
And sinners who never stop marveling at the grace of Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest story ever told does not need us to invent a better ending.
The tomb is already empty.
The Savior is already risen.
The invitation to repent and believe is already real.
And the grace of God in Jesus Christ is already greater than our words can contain.
Never add a sentence to God's silence when the truth He has spoken is already enough to lead a soul to Jesus.
